newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown outlines vision to boost prosperity.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown outlines vision to boost prosperity.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown on Thursday outlined his vision of how Britain could become more prosperous and said new approaches were needed to boost growth and jobs.
In his first Mansion House speech, a glittering set-piece event in the City of London, he said he hoped to set a lower inflation target than the present 2.5 percent in due course.

Brown also said his first budget next month would be for the long term, centring on a "welfare-to-work" programme to reduce unemployment, and he pledged to resist "irresponsible" public sector pay demands.

"Long-term investment holds the key to our future prosperity in Britain," the Chancellor said. "That is why I am determined to put in place the conditions that will encourage the high levels of investment we need."

Brown said the new Labour government was committed to monetary stability, fiscal stability, high levels of investment, "a long-term and far-reaching modernisation of the welfare state," free trade and Europe.
He dwelt in some detail on his reforms to monetary policy, which began within days of Labour's landslide May 1 election victory with his decision to let the Bank of England set interest rates.
"Progress has already been made in building our anti-inflation credibility. Long-term interest rates and inflation expectations have fallen," Brown said.

"Our new monetary framework is established on the basis of clear principles; it is for the long term, it sets clear rules and clear divisions of responsibility and it is open, transparent and accountable."
The Chancellor had earlier told parliament he was setting a target of 2.5 percent for annual underlying inflation, the same as that of the previous Conservative government.

But he added that if inflation deviated from the target by more than a percentage point in either direction, Bank of England Governor Eddie George would have to write a public letter explaining what had gone wrong and what he would do about it. That was the "final building block" in the new monetary framework, Brown said.

Brown, who disregarded years of tradition by not wearing "black tie" but a normal suit instead, said Britain had suffered the most volatile inflation reord of any of the Group of Seven leading industrial countries in the last 10 years and had the lowest investment as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP).
"If we succeed in strengthening the ability of the British economy to sustain growth with low inflation, and if international conditions permit, I would hope to lower the inflation target," he said.

As expected, Brown gave no clues as to the content of his first budget on July 2, saying only that it would "take the long-term view." "It will start from economic realities and challenges we face in a global market place where no-one owes us a living," he said.
"And with its concentration of welfare to work measures, it will take the first in a number of steps we are determined to take to modernise the welfare state and equip our country for the future."

The government aimed to achieve sustainable public finances for the long term and had already announced a comprehensive review of all government spending. It would borrow only to finance public investment, not to fund consumption.

In a shot across the bows of powerful public-sector trade unions which hope Labour will be more accommodating on pay than its Conservative predecessor, Brown said: "Just as we will resist any other irresponsible demand on public spending, we will resist irresponsible public sector pay demands."
Brown said a reformed welfare state that encouraged people to work was not only fair but would make for greater dynamism in the economy.

"The three modernisations we propose -- of employment policy, of tax and benefits and of lifelong learning -- reflect our determination not merely to compensate people for their poverty, but actually to tackle the causes of poverty by means that provide opportunity and so strengthen our economic performance," he said.

The Chancellor said the government wanted to play a leading role in shaping the future of Europe, pursuing "a British agenda for long-term success." It was working to overcome barriers to free trade in financial services in the European Union.
